# A National First: ONDCP's Inaugural Wastewater Report on Shifting Drug Signals


[Mariana Matus](https://substack.com/@marianamatus)


Sep 16, 2026


A few weeks ago, the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP) published the


[first-ever newsletter reporting wastewater-based drug use signals and trends](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/ONDCP-Wastewater-Newsletter-Issue-1-July-2026_FINAL.pdf) , drawn from more than 100 counties and covering roughly 18% of the U.S. population.


Thanks to the


[partnership with Biobot](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/biobot-analytics-selected-by-white-house-office-of-national-drug-control-policy-to-provide-nationwide-wastewater-intelligence-on-substance-use-trends-302654584.html) , t


his program represents the largest wastewater drug-monitoring effort in the country.


For those of us who have spent the better part of the last decade making wastewater intelligence the backbone of health security, this is a milestone worth reflecting on.


Wastewater drug signals across the U.S., April 2026. Source:


[ONDCP wastewater report](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/ONDCP-Wastewater-Newsletter-Issue-1-July-2026_FINAL.pdf)


### **Why this matters**


The U.S. drug supply continues to shift in ways that are difficult to detect through traditional public health reporting alone, underscoring the need for tools that can identify emerging substances before they become widespread.


No single data source — wastewater, ER visits, toxicology, or surveys — tells the whole story on its own; the value is in triangulating across all of them to get a fuller, faster picture of where the drug supply is heading.


### **Where this started**


My cofounder Newsha Ghaeli and I started Biobot in 2017 out of MIT with a simple, slightly strange idea: wastewater is not waste, but a health information highway. Biobot was born with the vision to transform wastewater infrastructure into human health observatories.


Biobot's wastewater intelligence platform initially focused on opioids like fentanyl and heroin, alongside medication-assisted treatments like naloxone, methadone, and buprenorphine. Our first pilot, run in North Carolina in 2018 with funding from the Bloomberg Mayors' Challenge, was a success — leading to community education campaigns and a measurable drop in overdoses (read more


[here](https://biobot.io/customer-success-story-biobot-and-cary-north-carolina/) and


[here](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31919800/) ).


That early proof point opened the door to federal backing: a 2020 SBIR Phase I/II award from NIH/NIDA to build out our technology platform, followed by a 2023 SBIR Phase III contract to pilot the work nationally — testing community buy-in for wastewater data on fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, xylazine, and naloxone across 76 sites in 41 states (read more


[here](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44221-026-00660-7.epdf?sharing_token=78WpFS9dKC5RP4YvROZjwNRgN0jAjWel9jnR3ZoTv0MjktHYJ2-_Pl1jqv1DiM054czOMWiipWuQolGxMAQYZsQzDzn0yvCsKpp4dPG-JwtcXgreh0Cscdt83qibk0Q3nmyGcirxTRxXMz6X409zmUfzTNo-FTvSAPykHiZQC34%3D) and


[here](https://www.mathematica.org/publications/new-uses-of-wastewater-data-on-high-risk-substances) ).


### **How it works**


The method is simpler than it sounds. Wastewater utilities collect a small sample of municipal wastewater: sewage that already represents the anonymous, combined biological signal of an entire community. Samples are analyzed in a lab using liquid chromatography mass spectrometry to detect drugs and their urinary metabolites.


Because sample size and flow vary site to site, we normalize results into population-weighted concentrations, so a small town and a major city can be compared on equal footing. The result is a trend line or index per community, not a data point about any individual.


### **How we keep this safe for communities**


Wastewater data is powerful precisely because it is aggregate and anonymous by design. Each sample represents thousands of people mixed together before it ever reaches a lab. We only collect samples at the community level, not in buildings, and work with federal and local government agencies to support public health and public safety.


### **What comes next**


Scaling substance monitoring nationally with a partner like ONDCP is exactly the kind of impact we set out to have when we founded Biobot: turning infrastructure that already exists beneath every American city and town into a human health observatory. We expect this to be the first of a regular cadence of national reporting, and we’re proud that our best-in-class platform is the engine behind it.


Stay tuned for more updates on our technology and partnerships supporting rapid response to the shifting drug supply.
